title: The Proclamation to the Gentiles
english: Preface to Galatians: After the Gentiles had accepted the preaching, some of the circumcised went out and tried to persuade the Gentiles to live like Jews. The first inquiry into this seems to have been held at Antioch, and the result was that the apostles wrote that the Gentiles were not to be bound by the law. They were only to keep away from food offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled and from fornication, “for so it seemed good to the Holy Spirit” (Acts 15:28–29). This sickness took hold of the Galatians, and they agreed together that they wanted to live like Jews. They had been talked into it by men who were leading them astray and claiming that the other apostles put no obstacle in the way of anyone who wanted to keep the law.
On Galatians 1:4: He shows that it was not Moses who died for the world, and not any other prophet either. So we must not give way to the one who did not save us, but to the one who died for us.
On Galatians 1:6–7: “To a different gospel, which is not another,” he says. For our gospel and the gospel of the apostles both want you free of the law.

On Galatians 1:8–10: An angel, granted; but why include “we”? When we preached, we preached in the power of the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit does not change his mind. So if we say something else, we have abandoned what belongs to the Spirit. Then let the preacher too be anathema, if he sets the preaching aside. “Contrary to what you received”: it is not, he says, that I preached and you failed to receive. I preached, and you received. I do not regret my preaching; so you must keep what you were given. “For am I now persuading men, or God? Or am I trying to please men? If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a slave of Christ.” He is about to remind them of his own gospel, so he guards himself in advance. He does not want them to think he is flattering them to win them over, because he is in fact striking at them as he warns them. By saying “if still,” he made it clear that he did once please men. Which men? The ones who gave him letters to harm the believers in Damascus (Acts 9:1–2). So, he says, if I were still pleasing the Jews, I would not have believed in Christ.

On Galatians 1:13: Why speak of his former life in Judaism at all? To show that he serves the truth, not a prejudice. He did not hate the law and so take shelter under grace; he was the law’s champion. He found what is perfect, and that is why he left the law. Now he shows that he has something beyond Peter and those with him: they were never zealots for Judaism who fought against the Christian faith, as I was. So do not imagine that I came to grace out of hatred for the law. I was the law’s defender. But I found what is perfect, and I will not rank the law with grace, which is perfect.
On Galatians 1:16: He does not say this to disparage the apostles. He means that he did not fall in line with mortal flesh.

On Galatians 2:16: No one is justified by works, which bring hard labour, but by faith, where both the ease and the righteousness are great. If so, he says, how can we avoid letting the law go and being content with grace? He says no one is justified by works of the law; he does not say “by commandments.” A commandment justifies when it is heeded; it was the work that was so hard to carry out.
